scenario: AITA For refusing to sit next to a kid with autism during a lecture, and sitting on the floor instead? | I know this sounds bad but bare with me, I’m (23m) in a class that has exactly 30 seats, and there are 31 students. I was running late and walked in a minute before the lecture began. There was only one open seat. I walked over to it and in the next seat over sitting was a kid with autism, he is very socially inept but totally brilliant. The problem is that he smelled like he hadn’t showered in a few weeks, his hair was greasier than Snapes, and he was wearing stained pajamas. I sat next to him for 2 minutes before I was about to gag and I got up and sat on the floor in the back of the lecture hall. The professor saw this and asked if I moved because of the smell, he asked in front of the whole class, I said I just didn’t want to sit there and he continued lecturing. After class a few of the kids said I was TA because I should have just sucked it up for the hour and dealt with the smell. So Reddit AITA?

Here’s why: 1. **Discrimination** The decision was based on the student’s disability (autism) and the way it manifests (social awkwardness, hygiene challenges). That’s a protected characteristic under most anti‑discrimination laws. Choosing to avoid him because of those traits is a form of bias. 2. **Social responsibility** In a shared space like a lecture hall, we’re all expected to be respectful of one another. If you’re uncomfortable, a better approach is to politely ask the professor for a different seat or to move to a different spot in the room. Sitting on the floor is a passive‑aggressive way to avoid the situation and can be seen as disrespectful to the student and to the class. 3. **Impact on the student** The student with autism is already navigating a world that can be overwhelming. Being singled out or ignored because of his appearance can add to that stress. It’s more supportive to treat him as you would any other classmate. 4. **Professionalism** The professor’s reaction—asking you in front of the whole class—was unprofessional. A better response would have been to offer you a different seat or to discuss the situation privately. That said, your discomfort is understandable, but the way you handled it was not the most constructive. 5. **Alternative solutions** • Ask the professor for a different seat before the lecture starts. • If you’re late and the only seat is next to the student, politely say you’d prefer to sit elsewhere and see if the professor can accommodate you. • If you’re truly uncomfortable, you could sit in the back or a different part of the room, but do so in a way that doesn’t single out the other student. In short, while it’s natural to feel uneasy about a situation that feels uncomfortable, refusing to sit next to someone because of their disability or appearance is discriminatory and unkind. A more respectful approach would involve communication with the professor and a willingness to share the space.
